chapter_theme: The first songs at Thiruthani (திருத்தணிகை): beside the usual confessions of courtesans who take a man's wealth, the poet catalogues his diseases, the body as a house of filth, the begging poet's humiliation and a child's plea to his father, and three songs name the Thiruppugazh itself; the praise dwells on Murugan as teacher of Siva and on Thani's blue-lily pool and fields.
structure_note: 240 is praise only. Courtesan confessions: 241, 252, 253, 254, with 242 on women's delusion. Diseases: 243, 250. The body and its tattvas: 244 (the pervading Siva), 247, 248. 245 confesses begging, 246 asks to worship, 249 to live among the singers of Thiruppugazh, 251 argues as a child to his father. 242, 249 and 254 name the Thiruppugazh.

240.reading: A song of praise: Siva, Vishnu and Brahma praise Murugan daily as six-faced Saravanabhava; he sent the vel like fire against the asuras, dwells by his anklet-ringed feet in devotees' hearts, was born of Uma, and as guru told Siva, to his delight, the meaning that ends the one word Pranava. All worlds, gods and sages praise him at Thanigai, where he comes with the hunter girl and the daughter of the heavenly tree at either side.
240.nuance: பரமன திருசெவி களிகூர உரைசெயு மொருமொழி பிரணவ முடிவதை: the teaching is spoken into Siva's ear and is the end (meaning) of Om, not the syllable alone. The song opens with the three gods as worshippers.

241.reading: The poet speaks of women who laugh softly, melt a man and wipe out his thought with dark eyes, draw him in and take all his wealth, and of men bound to them who boast of a tattva-knowledge found nowhere else; he asks whether he must slip again into this birth, lying down and rising in an instant. The praise names the vel that split the sea and the demons' mountain of illusion and took pity on Indra's city, the hunter girl, the cock banner, and the famous lily pool of Thiruthani.
241.nuance: ஒட்டறப் பொருட் பறிப்பவர், those who strip wealth entirely, are courtesans. The middle lines (தத்துவப் ப்ரசித்தி ... ஞானம் சமைத்துரைத்து) seem to mock those who contrive and proclaim a knowledge of the tattvas, but how they connect to the women, and the sense of the birth line, depend on a word split I am not sure of. உற்பலச் சுனை is the blue-lily pool of Thani.

242.reading: The poet recalls that those who read the Thiruppugazh with love are said to be freed of their troubles, and that men keep and recite the four kinds of poetry in music, dance, grammar and literature; without learning to recite it, he asks, must he fall into the delusion of clever women who melt men with breast, face and mind? The praise names Siva who burned Kama with the fire of his forehead eye, lives on Kailasa and gave half of himself to Uma, and Murugan as their son at Thiruthani.
242.nuance: The song names its own book: திருப்புகழ் விருப்பொடு படிப்பவர் இடுக்கினை அறுத்திடும், reading the Thiruppugazh with love cuts affliction. The burning of Kama (மதவேள்) in the praise answers the women of the plea. The opening word இருப்பவல் is unclear to me.

243.reading: The poet lists diseases, cough, epilepsy, wind, burning fevers, poison, urinary flux, headache, anaemia, scrofula, dropsy, phlegm and colic, and asks for Murugan's feet so that they do not torment him in birth after birth. The praise names the vel thrown while a crore of asuras died and Bhairavas danced, the husband of the girl given by Indra, and Thani hill with its lotus pool.
243.nuance: The plea is not to be cured now but to be spared the diseases in every birth (பிறவிகள் தோறும்), so the list stands for embodied life itself. முயலகன் is the epilepsy demon of the Siva story.

244.reading: The poet speaks of the light of lone knowledge that runs through the body, through the life that goes and returns, through awareness, sky, fire, wind, water and earth, through the crown of the four Vedas, the turiya state beyond, the form of Siva that does not join those who argue; and asks the Lord to tell a fool of endless desire and unremoved faults some means of touching it. The praise is a long scene of Thani's fields, where fish leap the sluices and flee the farmers into lotus pools, and names Murugan the guard of Thanigai, the mountain of compassion.
244.nuance: The repeated ஊடு, 'through', builds the pervasion line by line, from body and breath to the five elements and the Veda's end (நால்வேத முடி, Vedanta) to துரிய ... அதீத. வாதாடும் ஒருவரோடும் மேவாத, not joined to any who dispute, sets the truth apart from debate. The plea asks only for an உபாயம், a means. The text has nine corrupt glyphs, but ஊடு is clear throughout.

245.reading: The poet confesses that he searched out who the rich were, sang them extempore verses saying their fame was as great as Mount Meru, and walked back and forth until they said 'go, come tomorrow' and turned their faces; he asks for Murugan's two lotus feet before he is worn down. The praise names Siva with bull, trident, moon, vilva, skull, river and serpent in his matted hair, and Murugan who came in the toddling steps of wisdom while Siva watched and Uma rejoiced, at Thani hill of blue lilies.
245.nuance: ஆசுகவி, the quick verse made to order, is the poet's trade, and நாளை நடவும், 'go, tomorrow', its reward. ஞான தளர்நடை, the toddling child of wisdom before Siva and Uma, may point to Sambandar, whom the book identifies with Murugan; the text does not name him.

246.reading: The poet asks whether, never leaving the path of saving knowledge and reciting through the Veda, so that the darkness of delusion in the heart breaks and grace becomes his kin, he will worship Murugan at the hill of lilies with fresh vilva sprouts and scattered flowers. The praise names Murugan as son of Siva's consort and of Ganga, lord of the hunters, nephew of Vishnu, and plays on Devayanai's name: younger than the divine elephant, lord of the white elephant, dear to Devayanai.
246.nuance: The closing line puns three times on தெய்வ யானை: Ganapati the divine elephant, Indra's white elephant, and the goddess Devayanai. Much of the plea depends on how the rhythmic syllables split (மோகப்பொருளை, பழைய வல்ல), and I offer the reading only in outline.

247.reading: The poet runs through his bondage: how many arts, diseases, madnesses, inert things moving and unmoving, terrors, powers and attachments, and the daily satisfying of hunger with the flesh of killing; and asks that a madman so bound not perish thus but gain release, for the feet that stand beyond bondage. The praise is drum syllables and Thanigai, ringed by eight mountains, home of siddhas and hunters, red as the evening sky.
247.nuance: முத்தம் is release (mukti) and பெத்தம் bondage, Siddhanta terms set against each other. கொல் ஊனை நித்தம் பசியாறல, eating killed flesh daily, is the one concrete fault in the list. The lines on Murugan's seat (ஆசனத்தின் செயல்) and the garbled த்ததகுரு are beyond me.

248.reading: The poet calls the body a house of bones, nerves, blood, filth, brain, fat and worms, inhabited by many cheating tattvas, and describes the people who live in such houses, gamblers, householders in samsara, villains in the net of lust who never think of austerity, traitors to friends and killers, beset by fevers; he asks whether he must desire and carry this house and wander. The praise names the vel against Sura, Vishnu who slew Ravana, imprisoned Mahabali and cast the filed pestle into the sea, and Murugan as guru of his father after humbling Brahma, at Thiruthani.
248.nuance: The body is a வீடு, a house, and the tattvas within it சதிகாரர், conspirators. உலக்கை ராவி நடுக்கடல் விட்டவன் recalls the pestle ground to powder and thrown in the sea in the Yadava story. வலிக்க வேதனை குட்டி, knocking Brahma on the head, joins the Om story to பரப்ரமருக்கு அருள் குருநாதா.

249.reading: The poet confesses that he has gathered everything for himself, wearied without rest, and that the body he took dies without shame; to end his births he asks to live among those who speak of Murugan daily through the Thiruppugazh and never to part from the knowledge they teach, so that he too may worship his feet. The praise names the slaying of an opponent, the Veda Murugan told that pleased Brahma, the vel that took Sura's head, and the hunter girl, at Thiruthani.
249.nuance: திருப்புகழாலும் உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழி மேவி asks for the company of Thiruppugazh singers, so the book is again named within itself as a means of grace. The first line of the praise (வேள் கொன்றவன்) and the Brahma line are uncertain to me.

250.reading: The poet names leprosy, bile, fever, pain, epilepsy and cough, and asks not to die with his mind confused by thoughts of house, wife and children, but that Murugan come today on the emerald peacock and give him release. The praise names the vel that stands on the path to protect devotees, the chest that embraces the hunter girl, and Murugan who opened the prison where the asuras held the gods, at Thiruthani.
250.nuance: The disease list joins the family list: மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமை நினைந்து, and both are what the mind should not be clouded by at the end. முத்தி தரவேணும் asks for release directly.

251.reading: The poet argues with Murugan as a son: what wisdom has he, whom else can he seek, must he die in vain; Murugan is father and mother to him, and if he refuses to set his feet on him the world will laugh, for when a child runs crying before its father, who else picks it up, and would a father leave it to cry? The praise names the vel that drove off the villains of the eight directions like milk boiling over, Siva who danced with deer and axe, and Valli, at Thiruthani.
251.nuance: The plea is a lawyer's argument from kinship: பார் நகைக்கும், the world will laugh, if a father abandons his crying son. The grace is claimed as a father's duty, not begged as a favour.

252.reading: The poet describes women with palm-leaf earrings, picture-like colour, arrow eyes, sugared speech, bird voices, drum waists, garlands and pearl-hung breasts, whose deceitful delusion destroys the mind, who call a man into a dark room and, seizing his wealth, embrace him, and asks whether his suffering over them will not ease. The praise tells how Rama dried the sea, cut down Ravana's ten heads and freed Lakshmi from prison, names Murugan as his nephew and as son of Uma the parrot of dharma, the true guru who gives love to those who wear the ash, at Thiruthani.
252.nuance: இருட்டறை வாவெனப் பொருள் பற்றி முயக்கிடு, 'come into the dark room', seizing wealth and embracing, is the Kural's image of the courtesan's embrace almost word for word. நீறிட்டு நினைப்பவர், those who wear the ash and think of him, are the ones the true guru blesses.

253.reading: The poet describes women with bodiced breasts, pearls and jingling bangles who speak of infatuation and take the wealth in a man's hand, and calls himself a slave of desire, melted and ignorant, who does not know the one thing that has no remainder; he asks for Murugan's fragrant feet now. The praise names Krishna who stole curd from the cowherd women and came on Garuda, and Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent as uncle, at Thani hill praised by Siva.
253.nuance: கைப்பொருள் கவர்தரு, taking the wealth in hand, marks the courtesans. எச்சமில் ஒருபொருள், the one thing without remainder, names what the poet does not know against what the women take. The line on the bird (குற்கிர வினியொடு) is unclear to me.

254.reading: The poet describes women who trouble those who come near with a sidelong glance, call them, speak the arts of love, melt the heart with bird cries, loosen their silk, take a man to bed, kiss, bind him in their hair, mark him with nails and teeth and keep him in their laps, and asks whether he must delight in them. The praise names Murugan who gave life to the Thiruppugazh that tames adversity, the vel of the millet hill, the cock banner, and the true guru who taught the Unborn Siva and ended false babble, at Thiruthani of paddy heaps.
254.nuance: மெய்ப்பொருள் திருப்புகழ்க்கு உயிர்ப்பளித்து makes Murugan the giver of the book's life, the third song of the chapter to name it. பிறப்பிலிக்கு உணர்த்து சற்குரு, the true guru who taught the Unborn, is the Siva-teaching story without naming Om.

links.note: Both put the courtesan's embrace for money in a dark room (இருட்டறை). The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse; 252 keeps the room and the seized wealth but not the corpse, and confesses the pull instead of warning.

Both take the body apart into bone, blood, fat and entrails to break desire. The Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman; 248 turns the inventory on the poet's own body, a house he still longs to carry.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons in Tamil for gifts; 245 adds the rebuff, 'come tomorrow' and the turned face, and asks, like 15, for the feet instead.
Both are catalogues of diseases set as the plea; 232 ties them to sin and women, while 243 asks to be spared them in every birth.
Both name the Thiruppugazh within itself as a means of grace: 242 says reading it cuts affliction, 249 asks to live among those who sing it.

Tirumular says the eaters of flesh are seized by Yama's messengers and thrown into hell; 247 counts the daily eating of killed flesh among the bonds and asks for release from them, without the threat.

The Tirumanthiram's adept takes the teaching that is Om (பிரணவமாம் உபதேசத்தை) into a true heart and stands as servant of the Father (அத்தற்கு அடிமை). 240 tells the same Om-teaching with the roles turned: the son, as guru, speaks the end of the one word Om (ஒருமொழி பிரணவ முடிவதை) into the ear of the Father, Siva (பரமன திருசெவி களிகூர). The pairing shows the pranava upadesa running downward from Siva in one book and upward to him in the other.

The Kural likens death to falling asleep and birth to waking (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு ... விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு). 241 asks whether he must again gain this birth that slips past in a blink, lying down and rising (இமைப்பினிற் சடக்கெனப் படுத்தெழச் சறுக்கும் இப்பிறப்பு). The song takes the Kural's calm image of sleep and waking and makes it the speed with which a birth is lost.

The Tirumanthiram says those who rise in the morning and recite Mulan's three thousand Tamil verses knowing their meaning (கருத்தறிந்து ஓதிடின்) will reach the Lord of the world. 242 recalls that those who read the Thiruppugazh with love (திருப்புகழ் விருப்பொடு படிப்பவர்) have their affliction cut. Both books promise a fruit for reciting the book itself, one asking for understanding, the other for love.

The Tirumanthiram says he is awareness and life, the senses and union, yet cannot be reached by thought (உணர்வும் அவனே உயிரும் அவனே ... எண்ணலும் ஆகான்). 244 traces the same light of knowledge through life and awareness (உயிரினூடு ... உணர்வினூடு) and on through the elements to turiya, then asks only for some means of touching it (தொடும் உபாயம் ஏதோ). The song takes the pervasion the Tirumanthiram states and turns its 'cannot be thought' into a plea for a way.

The Naladiyar ranks as the lowest life following, for desire of wealth, people who do not recognise one's worth (பொருள்நசையால் தம்மை உணரார்பின் சென்று நிலை). 245 confesses exactly that life: seeking out who the rich were, singing them quick verses (ஆசு கவிபாடி), and walking back and forth until they said 'come tomorrow' and turned their faces (நாளை நடவுமென ... முகம்வேறாய்). The song gives the scene of humiliation that the Naladiyar's ranking only names.

The Kural says that grace is not killing and its absence is killing, and eating that flesh is not right (அவ்வூன் தினல் பொருளல்லது). 247 lists among the bonds that keep him from release the daily satisfying of hunger with killed flesh (கொலூனை நித்தம் பசியாறல்), set against mukti (முத்தம்) and bondage (பெத்தம்). The pairing shows the Kural's ethical rule placed by the song inside the Siddhanta scheme of bondage and release.

The Kural asks whether the life that lodges in the body as a temporary shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has found no home of its own. 248 calls the body a house (வீடு) of bones, blood, filth and worms, full of conspiring tattvas, and asks whether he must desire and carry that house and wander (வீடதை நத்தி எடுத்து இவண் உழல்வேனோ). Both use the image of the body as a dwelling the soul does not truly own; the song adds the disgust and the tenants.

The Naladiyar says that even the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain good sense day by day (கற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகின் நல்லறிவு நாளுந் தலைப்படுவர்), like water taking the scent of pathiri flowers. 249 asks to live among those who speak of Murugan daily through the Thiruppugazh (உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழி மேவி) and never to part from the knowledge they impart (உணர்த்திய போதந் தனைப் பிரியாது). The pairing shows the Naladiyar's rule of learning by company applied to the company of devotees.

The Naladiyar rebukes the heart that will not let go of the bond of home and pines for children (மனைப்பாசம் கைவிடாய் மக்கட்கென்று ஏங்கி), as though it would live for ages. 250 asks not to die with his mind clouded by thoughts of house, wife and children (மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமை நினைந்து ... மடியாதே), and for release now. Both name house and children as the attachment that holds at the end; the Naladiyar's remedy is good deeds, the song's is Murugan's coming today.

251 argues that a father does not let a son run crying before him and leave him to cry (அப்பன்முன் மைந்தனோடிப் ... அழ பார்விடுப்பர்களோ), so Murugan, as father and mother, must take him. The Tirumanthiram also makes the Lord a parent of sons, but one who has seen their tendencies and faults (நாற்றமும் குற்றமுங் கண்டு) and deals with each by its nature, without anger (உயிரது பான்மைக்குச் செற்றமிலாச் செய்கை). The pairing adds a condition to the song's claim: the father's care is fitted to the child's nature, not only drawn by its crying.

The Naladiyar mocks those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), saying many will laugh at them. 253 describes women who take the wealth in a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கவர்தரு) and calls himself a slave of desire and a fool (அறிவிலி) for melting before them. The song speaks in the first person the folly the Naladiyar sees in others, with the same word for the taking.

source_issues: Song 243: one corrupt character in லு஡ர்தி (line 13); clearly ஊர்தி.

Song 244: nine corrupt characters; ஡ stands for ஊ in the repeated ஊடு (னு஡டு, வானு஡டு, யாறு஡டு), and ஡ண for ரீ in வா஡ணச (line 9), probably வாரீச (lotus). Also unflagged நநருடு (line 3), probably நீருடு, the sign seen in songs 21 and 33.
Song 247: one corrupt character in கொலு஡னை (line 4); probably கொல் ஊனை. Also unflagged த்ததகுரு (line 7), unclear.
